units.translation: But whether I happen to, I do not know.
Let us see whether anything of this prelude is in vain.
Tell me first whether you killed your mother.
Explain to me whether I killed her justly.
I lament with mournful flowers, fearing for my loved ones, whether there is any protector of this exile.
A terrifying fear truly holds me, whether there is any help for me in my far-wandering exile.
Whether with armed men, or even alone.
Judge the case, whether justly or not.
Whether justly or not, judge this blood according to your judgment.
Whether you wish to benefit the dead or harm them, it is possible either way.
they would fare as best as possible
I would not find an end
Come on, dear comrades in arms, this task is not far off.
Come on, let everyone make ready his sword with hilt forward.

Thus Hermann for δακρυσίστακτον δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν λειβομένα [dripping with tears from her slender eyes]. The same corruption in Sophocles Ant. 527 Ισμήνη, φιλάδελφα κάτω δάκρυα λειβόμενα [Ismene, shedding sisterly tears below], where Triclinius correctly has δάκρυ᾽ εἰβομένη [shedding tears].
Dripping with tears from her slender eyes, she wet her cheek with moist streams.
dripping with tears from her slender eyes
And the unconquerable divinity, appearing like her parents.
Not blameworthy in form, nor in spirit, nor in the bearing of his arms.
Bronze is a mirror of the form, but wine of the mind.

Schol. Hom. Od. 4, 366 Εἰδοθέη: ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδήσεως καὶ ἐπιστήμης τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ ὄνομα. καὶ Αἰσχύλος δὲ ἐν Πρωτεῖ [Eidothea: the name comes from the knowledge and understanding of her father. And Aeschylus in Proteus] (fr. 210) Εἰδοθέαν αὐτὴν καλεῖ [calls her Eidothea]. Etym. Gud. p. 316, 30 corrected from cod. Paris. 2638, κερδώ: ὑποκοριστικῶς, ὡς παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ ἡ Εἰδὼ καὶ Ὑψὼ ἀντὶ τοῦ Εἰδοθέα καὶ Ὑψιπύλη [kerdo: as a diminutive, as in Aeschylus Ido and Hypso instead of Eidothea and Hypsipyle]. Cf. Bekker's Anecdota p. 857, 9 and schol. Aristoph. Eq. 1065 (1068). From these it can be gathered that Aeschylus did not say Eidothea, as the Homeric scholium reports, but Ido.
Eidothea: the name comes from the knowledge and understanding of her father. And Aeschylus in Proteus
kerdo: as a diminutive, as in Aeschylus Ido and Hypso instead of Eidothea and Hypsipyle
A mirror of companionship, a phantom of a shadow.
third person plural of the optative εἴην, which has become an adverb, which can be rendered in Latin as esto, age.

where it should be noted that εἶεν [well then] is placed at the beginning of a trimeter as a spondee, in what seems to be a solemn formula. In the same way in Aristophanes Pac. 663 εἶεν, ἀκούω · ταῦτ᾽ ἐπικαλεῖς; μανθάνω [well then, I hear; do you bring these charges? I understand]. For thus the best manuscripts and the scholiast, the inferior ones εἶέν γ', ἀκούω [well then, I hear].
